claims.text: Retention or loss of toughness in high-entropy alloys is governed by the evolution and coherency of nanoprecipitates.
Coherent nanoprecipitates maintain or enhance toughness by facilitating dislocation transmission and mitigating stress concentrations.
Incoherent or brittle second phases degrade toughness.
The proposed initial HEA can have a predominantly single-phase, homogeneous microstructure without significant precipitate formation.
Stepwise controlled thermal treatment can induce controllable coherent nanoprecipitation in a tungsten refractory HEA.
Slightly altered heat-treatment conditions can selectively produce incoherent or brittle precipitate phases instead of coherent nanoprecipitates.
Thermal exposures at 700–1000 °C for suitable durations permit precipitate nucleation and growth while allowing precipitate coherency to be varied.
Nanoprecipitate coherency mediates local dislocation dynamics and stress distribution.
Coherent precipitate interfaces facilitate dislocation transmission and relieve stress concentrations associated with premature crack initiation.
Coherent nanoprecipitates prevent crack initiation by enabling smoother dislocation motion.
Incoherent precipitates act as stress concentrators that promote early crack initiation and reduce deformation energy absorption.
Specimens containing predominantly coherent nanoprecipitates will maintain or improve toughness relative to an untreated baseline.
A higher proportion of incoherent precipitates will cause a measurable decrease in toughness.
The untreated or minimally heat-treated, uniform single-phase HEA has moderate toughness.
The proposed coherency–toughness mechanism applies to both FCC and refractory multi-principal-element alloys when phase stability permits controlled precipitation.
The mechanism may not apply when phase transformations generate entirely deleterious microstructures.
Critical precipitate size, volume fraction, and coherency thresholds for preserving toughness are not quantified and may vary with alloy system and thermal history.

contradictions.description: The prediction allows unchanged toughness to count as successful retention, whereas the falsification rule says that failure to obtain a statistically significant toughness improvement falsifies the hypothesis.
